I looked at the general arrangement this morning. Why did you go for concrete on the main frame? I would have expected steel.
Mainly the load. The process equipment on the first floor is far heavier than a normal industrial load, and the client may add more later.
Fair. But a steel frame would be considerably faster to erect. You are losing weeks on site.
We are. That is the trade-off. But at an eighteen-metre span, the difference is much smaller than it looks, and the foundation cost is nearly the same either way.
And the external walls? Are you doing masonry?
No. Precast panels on three faces. They are by far the quickest option, and the durability in a humid process area is significantly better than block.
That makes sense. What about the east face, next to the loading bay?
Metal cladding there, because the client wants to be able to open that wall in five years. It is not as durable, but it is the only one we can remove.
Concrete is only slightly heavier on the foundations.
The trade-off is four weeks on site, in exchange for future load capacity.
Masonry is nowhere near as durable as concrete in a humid process area.

People always start this conversation with cost, and cost is almost never what decides it. The first question I ask is the load, and the second is the span. If the equipment on the floor is much heavier than a normal industrial load, or if the client is likely to add equipment in three years, concrete gives me room that steel does not, unless I oversize the frame from the start. Beyond about twenty-five metres of span, that reverses, and steel wins almost every time. Then, and only then, we talk about money. And when somebody says one option is cheaper, I always ask cheaper over what. The frame is a small part of the total. A frame that is fifteen percent cheaper and four weeks slower on site is not cheaper at all, and a frame that is slightly more expensive but needs a simpler foundation often is.

On that plant we compared block masonry with precast panels, and the panels saved about seven weeks. That was the number everybody quoted in the meeting. But it is not why we chose them. The client had two older buildings on the same site, both in block, and in the humid process areas the block was performing badly after eight years. So the argument that actually won was durability, not speed. Speed was just the part that was easy to put in a table. I will say the honest disadvantage too, because people forget it. Panels are much harder to change later. Every opening, every door, every penetration has to be decided before the mould is made. With block you can cut a hole in year three and nobody cries. With panels you cannot, so the design has to be genuinely finished, and on a fast project that is a real cost.

I sit in a lot of design reviews, and the comparisons that fail all fail the same way. Somebody shows a table with two columns, six advantages on each side, and then stops. Nobody in the room can decide anything from that, so the meeting goes round for forty minutes and ends with a request for more information. What I want in the first thirty seconds is three things. Your recommendation. The one reason behind it, not the six. And the thing you are giving up, said out loud by you, before somebody else finds it. The third one is what makes people trust the first two. And please do not use the word better on its own. Better is not an argument. Better at what, and by how much? Slightly cheaper and significantly slower is a sentence a room can decide on. Better is a sentence that starts another meeting.
